body.text: Japan may come to remember Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s first visit to China as leader as the “humiliation of Shenzhen.” Takaichi went to the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit seeking talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. She shook his hand twice but came home without a bilateral meeting.

At the Shenzhen airport, Takaichi steadied herself against her government aircraft as she stepped down onto boarding stairs that were about 40 centimeters below the door. Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru said Japanese officials knew about the gap beforehand and took safety precautions. It remains unclear whether the gap at Takaichi’s exit was created intentionally.

A former Japan Airlines captain who reviewed the footage for Fuji Television said the stairs appeared high enough at first and seemed to be lowered in stages as they were lined up with the aircraft. He described the adjustment as highly unusual. A Fuji Television reporter aboard the same aircraft said there was no noticeable step down at the exit used by the press.

By contrast, Xi personally greeted U.S. President Donald Trump at the airport. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. received music, flowers, and dancing despite Manila’s disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea. Taiwan’s APEC representative, Stan Shih, and his wife had a quieter welcome. There was no music or dancing, but children greeted them with flowers.

Takaichi received none of those celebratory touches. Besides the stair debacle, she was met by Zhang Qiyue, a former Chinese ambassador to Greece serving as a protocol envoy. China’s Foreign Ministry said its arrangements followed international practice.

At the banquet, the hosts played “Ue o Muite Arukō,” the Sakamoto Kyu hit known abroad as “Sukiyaki.” Its lyricist, Ei Rokusuke, took part in the 1960 protests against the revision of the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty. That history gave the choice an ironic resonance for a prime minister who has made the alliance central to her diplomacy.

Chinese officials may have toned down the welcome to avoid appearing too accommodating toward Japan. They may have been anticipating their superiors’ wishes while trying to avoid a backlash from nationalists online. Other signals, however, suggested the snubbing came from the top. Beijing received Takaichi as an APEC participant and gave her no opportunity for formal talks with Xi.

On November 19, Takaichi spoke to Xi for about 10 seconds during their second handshake. He appeared to nod, and but it’s unclear from the footage whether he actually gave a verbal reply. Takaichi stood second from the right in the back row of the official group photo.

It was a stark contrast from the previous APEC summit in Gyeongju, South Korea, when Xi met Takaichi for the first time. In their summit on October 31, 2025, the two leaders agreed to work toward stable ties.

Just a week later, Takaichi told parliament that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could, under certain conditions, qualify as a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, a legal threshold that can permit the use of force. Previous Japanese prime ministers had left open how Japan might respond.

From Beijing’s perspective, the timing made the remarks a personal embarrassment for Xi. He had just met Japan’s new prime minister and publicly backed stable ties, only to hear her confirm that Japan might use force in a Taiwan crisis. Beijing demanded a retraction, which was not forthcoming, and ties have been a deep freeze ever since.
In Shenzhen, Takaichi reaffirmed Japan’s position on Taiwan under the 1972 Japan-China joint communiqué.

The dispute also brought a deeper divide over Japan’s wartime past back into view. Beijing still sees Japan’s reckoning with its wartime aggression as a foundation of bilateral ties. Takaichi’s record on historical issues, including her visits to Yasukuni Shrine, is part of her appeal to conservative supporters. These differences make it harder for her and Xi to rebuild trust.

On March 16, 1995, Takaichi, a staunch conservative, told the lower house Foreign Affairs Committee that she felt no personal remorse over the war and saw no reason to be asked to express it, since her generation had played no part in the war. Then-Foreign Minister Kono Yohei disagreed.

A China-based specialist on China-Japan relations told me in May that public hostility toward Takaichi in China left her little room to win back goodwill. When I asked him again on November 19, he said Beijing regards Taiwan as an internal matter and would continue to push back against Japanese remarks on the issue. “China will take its time and wait for a turning point,” he said.

Beijing’s cold reception may make that turning point harder to reach. If it stirs sympathy for Takaichi in Japan, any move that looks like giving ground becomes more costly for her. In China, a warmer approach risks looking like a retreat on Taiwan.

China-Japan relations also experience a deep freeze under Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, who sparked Chinese ire when he visited the controversial Yasukuni Shrine in 2013. Yet Abe’s diplomacy with China showed the value of keeping channels open during a dispute. Former Prime Minister Fukuda Yasuo met Xi ahead of Abe’s first summit with him in 2014. In 2017, Liberal Democratic Party Secretary-General Nikai Toshihiro delivered a personal letter from Abe to Xi.

In Shenzhen, Trump held his own talks with Xi and joined a separate meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump later briefed Takaichi by phone, but Tokyo still needs a way to make its own case directly to Beijing.

A sharp downturn in China-U.S. relations could give Beijing more reason to seek Japanese trade, investment, or diplomatic cooperation. For now, Trump and Xi are working to stabilize their relationship, and China can afford to wait. As long as Takaichi and Xi remain in office, a lasting thaw in China-Japan ties looks remote.
